title: The wrong prescription for liberal democracy's ills
gist: Marc Levinson reviews Daron Acemoglu's 'What Happened to Liberal Democracy?' and argues its call for a 'working-class liberalism' misdiagnoses the problem: liberal democracy's legitimacy rested on postwar productivity growth, and the post-1973 productivity slump, which no government of any stripe could reverse, is the root cause of voter alienation. He finds Acemoglu US-centric, unconvincing on regulation, and odd as an economist in proposing to cut investment tax incentives and curb automation, while noting his 'pro-worker AI' idea has won wide applause.

themes.theme: Productivity as the foundation of democratic legitimacy

insights.claim: Postwar liberal democracy's appeal rested largely on delivering the goods: rapid income growth driven by strong productivity growth in western Europe, North America and Japan through the 1950s and 1960s.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Political stability in democracies is tightly linked to visible productivity-driven income growth.
insights.quote: The attraction of postwar liberalism was based largely on its ability to deliver the goods.

insights.claim: After the 1973 oil shock and the 1975 end of the recession, productivity growth slumped and liberal democracies could not restore the growth that underpinned their legitimacy, triggering a shift right to Reagan, Thatcher and Kohl.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Supply shocks that permanently lower productivity can reshape political regimes and policy for decades.
insights.quote: liberal democracies found themselves powerless to restore the economic growth that underpinned their legitimacy

insights.claim: Levinson argues the underlying cause of democratic alienation is a steep drop in productivity growth, which public officials lack the tools to address, so right-wing governments did no better than centrist or left ones.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Investors should treat productivity growth (e.g. from AI) as the key variable for political stability and populism risk.
insights.quote: is not something public officials have tools to address
insights.locator: Right-wing governments proved no more able

insights.claim: The post-1970s shift moved costs and risks of health care, education, unemployment and old age onto individuals, weakened unions and shifted the tax burden from corporations to wage earners, so asset-rich families fared well while working-class families stagnated.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Explains the asset-holder vs wage-earner divide that fuels populist demand for redistribution or capital taxation.
insights.quote: Families with significant financial assets fared well, while working-class families trod water.

insights.claim: Sarah Longwell argues voters judge democracy by its fruits, not its roots, caring more about petrol prices than constitutional norms ahead of the November congressional election.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Fuel and cost-of-living outcomes, not institutional concerns, will drive US midterm results.
insights.quote: Voters know democracy by its fruits, not its roots.

themes.theme: Global erosion of the political centre

insights.claim: Leaders openly disrespectful of democratic institutions are in power from Turkey to India to Argentina, while centrist parties are in trouble almost everywhere.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Broad centrist erosion raises policy volatility and institutional risk across markets.

insights.claim: Two thirds of German voters support none of the three parties that have framed German political debate for nearly 80 years.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Fragmentation of Germany's party system raises governance and fiscal policy uncertainty in Europe's largest economy.
insights.quote: Two thirds of German voters support none of the three parties that have framed political debate in Germany for nearly 80 years

insights.claim: Trump has imposed sweeping tariffs, bombed Iran and torn down half the White House without congressional consent, and governs via executive orders and agency regulations despite his party controlling Congress.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Executive-driven policy (tariffs, military action) creates abrupt policy shocks without legislative signalling.

insights.claim: Liberal democracy's heyday was brief: most 1920s democracies fell to authoritarianism by the early 1930s, and it only took firm root around 1948.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Democratic durability is historically contingent on economic performance.

insights.claim: Acemoglu argues that a college-educated elite abandoned self-government, community and shared prosperity and engaged in 'supply-driven social engineering', calling instead for a 'working-class liberalism'.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: An influential Nobel economist is legitimising an anti-technocratic, pro-worker policy agenda.

insights.claim: Levinson counters that falling wage share cannot explain anti-liberal politics, since authoritarian-rooted parties have risen in India, Serbia and Sweden where the wage share has not fallen.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Redistribution alone may not defuse populist risk; wage share is driven by tax and union policy choices.
insights.quote: parties with authoritarian roots have also challenged liberal democracy in countries where the wage share has not fallen
insights.locator: Nor are they as widely applicable

insights.claim: Regulation via specialised agencies can adapt quickly to rapid technological change, whereas legislatures take years; AI copyright disputes show technology outpacing law.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Expect AI governance to come mainly through agency rule-making rather than slow legislation.
insights.quote: AI is developing far faster than copyright law

insights.claim: Emissions taxes are no simpler to enact than regulation: the EU emissions trading scheme exempts fishing boats, commercial printers, most textile mills and other industries due to political jockeying.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Carbon pricing is riddled with carve-outs, limiting its effective coverage.
insights.locator: What is the evidence that regulations

insights.claim: Many liberal democracies have curtailed coal and oil burning through generous subsidies for solar, wind, batteries and EVs rather than relying on carbon taxes.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Subsidy-led energy transition remains the dominant policy model, supporting clean-tech demand.
insights.locator: What is the evidence that regulations

insights.claim: Levinson calls the book a disappointment, arguing its self-flagellating critique of liberals is unlikely to make democracy's fruits more apparent to voters.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Narrative fixes will not address the productivity-driven sources of political discontent.

insights.claim: Acemoglu calls for governments to push 'pro-worker AI' focused on domain-specific tools that raise worker capabilities and wages rather than mimicking human cognition and eliminating jobs; the idea has drawn wide applause.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: Signals potential policy pressure favouring augmentation-oriented AI over labour-replacing AI.
insights.quote: Pro-worker AI has the capacity to boost productivity, rebuilding the link between productivity growth and good jobs

insights.claim: Acemoglu proposes reducing generous tax incentives for business investment in computers and machinery, such as US full first-year expensing, to fight wage inequality, putting him at odds with most economists.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: If adopted, curbing expensing would raise after-tax capex costs for manufacturers and tech buyers.
insights.locator: A recommendation likely to prove more controversial

insights.claim: Acemoglu breaks with economic consensus by criticising automation for severing the link between mass production and shared prosperity, which Levinson calls a strange argument for an economist.
insights.speaker: Marc Levinson
insights.so_what: An anti-automation strand of elite economic thought could inform labour-friendly regulation affecting automation and AI vendors.
insights.quote: because it severs the link between mass production and shared prosperity
